title: Why Has My Sharpening Stone Stopped Cutting?
thumbnail_text: Your stone is not dead. It is clogged.

scenes.heading: Why Has My Sharpening Stone Stopped Cutting?
scenes.sub: Two faults, two fixes, and when to replace it
scenes.narration: If your sharpening stone has stopped cutting, you will learn here exactly why, and how to fix it. It is almost always one of two things. Either the face is loaded with steel dust and has gone slick, or it has worn hollow in the middle and is no longer flat. Loading is far more common. It looks just like a worn out stone, and five minutes with soapy water puts it right. Dishing is the serious one, because a stone that is not flat cannot grind a flat edge, however careful you are. Most skaters are never taught this part. They learn the jig and the passes, then blame their technique when the edge stops coming up.

scenes.heading: Which problem do you have?
bullets: Feels slick, not grippy: loaded
Grey smear on the blade: loaded
Burr takes far longer: test for both
Light under a rule: dished
Block flexes or cracked: replace it
scenes.narration: Do not reach for a flattening plate before you know what you are dealing with. The two faults feel different on the blade, and the fix for one does nothing for the other. If the stone feels slick rather than grippy, or leaves a greyish smear on the steel, it is loaded. Scrub it clean and try again. If a burr takes far longer than usual to come up, it could be either, so clean it first and then check it for flat. If light shows under a straight rule laid on the face, or your corners come up rounded however careful you are, the stone is dished. And if the block flexes, rattles in your hand or has cracked, it is finished. Replace it.

scenes.heading: Loading: the fake worn out stone
bullets: Steel dust packs into the pores
The grains can no longer reach the blade
It polishes instead of cutting
Common in stones under a season old
scenes.narration: Loading happens because every pass fills the pores of the stone with the metal it has just removed. Fine steel particles pack into the surface until the abrasive grains cannot reach the blade. At that point the stone stops cutting and starts burnishing. It polishes the steel instead of removing any. That is why a loaded stone can leave a blade looking brighter while the corners stay just as round as before. The signs are consistent. The face feels slippery instead of biting. It leaves a dull grey smear. And the burr takes two or three times as long to appear, or never arrives. If your stone is less than a season old and has gone lifeless, this is almost certainly the cause. Nothing is wrong with the block itself.

scenes.heading: Flat stone versus dished stone
scenes.chapter: How a hollow stone rounds corners
scenes.narration: Dishing is uneven wear. You press hardest through the middle of each stroke and ease off at the ends, so the centre of the stone loses material faster. Over time the face becomes a shallow hollow. Look at the two stones here, seen end on. On the left, a flat stone meets the blade across its full width, and it leaves a flat bottom with two square corners. On the right, the dished stone only touches the blade at its high shoulders. Those shoulders take the cut, right at the corners of the blade. So an hour of careful work gives you a curved bottom and rolled corners, the exact edge you sat down to remove.

scenes.heading: The straight edge check
bullets: Use a steel rule or straight edge
Never use a skate blade for this
Hold it up to a lamp or window
Check along the length and across
scenes.narration: Checking for flat takes about ten seconds and no measuring tools. Lay something you trust to be straight along the working face. A steel rule or an engineer's straight edge is ideal. Do not use a blade, however true you think it is. Short track steel is rockered along its length, so on a perfectly flat stone it shows light at both ends. That could fool you into flattening a good stone for nothing. Hold the rule and the stone up against a window or a lamp and look at the join. Then turn the rule across the width and look again. Stones wear in both directions, and a face can be true along its length while hollow across it.

scenes.heading: What the light tells you
scenes.narration: Here is what you are looking for. On the left, no light shows between the straight edge and the stone. The face is flat, so carry on sharpening. On the right, a thin sliver of light shows in the middle and closes at both ends. That face is dished, and it needs flattening before it touches a blade again. Run this check every second or third sharpening session, and always in the week before a competition. It is the cheapest insurance in your kit bag. It also explains a lot of weekends where nothing felt right and nobody could say why.

scenes.heading: Cleaning a loaded stone
bullets: Wet it, scrub with a nylon brush
A drop of washing up liquid helps
Nylon pad, never steel wool
Rinse all slurry, dry it fully
scenes.narration: Cleaning a loaded stone is a five minute job at the kitchen sink. Wet the face and work it over with a stiff nylon brush or an old toothbrush, along the length and then across the width. If the grey will not lift, add a little washing up liquid. Soap helps release metal that water alone leaves behind. Use a firm nylon pad, not steel wool, because loose steel fibres are the last thing you want in an abrasive face. Rinse away all the slurry, including what sits at the edges. Then stand the stone on edge and let it dry completely. Test it on a blade you are not precious about. To prevent loading, wipe the face before you start and when you finish, and clear the dust as it builds up.

scenes.heading: Flattening a dished stone
bullets: Lap it on a wet diamond plate
Even pressure, circles or figure eights
Rotate the stone as you go
Rinse the slurry away often
scenes.narration: If the straight edge shows light, bring the face back to level before you sharpen again. The idea is simple. Rub the worn face against something flat and more abrasive than the stone, until the hollow is gone. A diamond plate is the tidiest tool and the most likely to give a truly flat result. Wet the plate and lay the stone on it. Work in overlapping circles or figures of eight with even pressure, and rotate the stone every so often so one end is not always loaded. Rinse the slurry away as it builds. Trapped slurry slows the cut, and loose silicon carbide is hard on a diamond plate.

scenes.heading: Use a pencil grid
scenes.narration: This trick makes the job visible. First, draw a pencil grid across the whole working face. Second, lap and look. The high ends are cut first and lose their marks, while the hollow middle keeps them. Third, when every square has gone, the whole face is level, so stop. Work the whole face, not just the middle. That is the instinct, and it is exactly wrong, because the middle is already too low. Check with the straight edge as you go and stop the moment it reads flat. Every pass costs stone you never get back. If a block is heavily worn, a workshop with a surface grinder is a fair alternative.

scenes.heading: Wet, dry, and no oil
bullets: Follow the guidance for your stone
Do not oil a stone not sold as one
Oil traps steel in the pores
Water and a drop of soap is enough
scenes.narration: Follow whatever guidance came with your stone, because different blocks are made to be used differently. A stone meant for dry use does not improve with soaking. Whatever you own, the essentials are the same. Keep the face clean and flat, wipe the steel dust away as it appears, and make sure the stone is bone dry before it goes back in your bag. Do not improvise with oil on a stone that was not sold as an oilstone. Oil holds metal in the pores instead of letting it rinse out. A couple of sessions can turn a stone you could have rinsed clean into one that needs degreaser. Plain water, or water with a drop of soap, is all most speed skating stones want.

scenes.heading: When to replace it
bullets: Thin enough to flex or wobble
Cracked anywhere
Hollow too deep to flatten
Check both faces of a combination stone
scenes.narration: A mildly dished stone is worth saving. Replace it instead when the block is thin enough to flex or sit unstable under your hand, when it has cracked, or when flattening would eat most of what is left. A stone too thin to stay rigid follows the blade instead of correcting it. Check both faces while you are at it. The two sides of a combination stone wear separately, so the coarse side you rarely use can be dished without you noticing. In a warm, humid climate, also watch for moisture. A damp stone in a closed kit bag means rust on everything it touched. Dry everything, store the stone flat, and keep it apart from your blades if you can.

scenes.heading: A flat stone before a sharp blade
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: Every edge you own is a copy of the surface that made it. Keep the stone clean so it cuts. Keep it flat so it cuts square. Dry it before it goes away, and check both faces often enough to find a problem before your blades do. The full guide on the LiveLica blog also covers caring for your deburr stone, polishing triangle and jig, plus answers to common questions. Find it at the link in the description.
